nameStory: Springs clearweed gets its name from its love of moist, spring-fed areas where water bubbles up from the ground. The 'clearweed' part comes from its transparent, watery stems that you can almost see through when you hold them up to the light. Unlike its stinging nettle cousins, this gentle plant won't leave you with an itchy surprise!
description: Springs clearweed is a small, delicate annual herb that rarely grows taller than a foot. It has a soft, succulent appearance with translucent green stems and oval leaves that feel smooth and slightly fleshy to the touch. The tiny flowers are so small you might miss them entirely - they're greenish and clustered along the stems without any showy petals. This humble little plant prefers to stay in the shadows of wetland edges and spring seeps.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Translucent, watery-looking stems that feel soft and succulent, almost like you could squish water out of them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, smooth leaves arranged opposite each other on the stem, with a slightly fleshy texture and prominent veining

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers in small clusters - so small you need to look closely to see them at all

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling annual that stays close to moist ground, rarely exceeding 12 inches tall

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, teardrop-shaped seeds about 1/8 inch long that feel papery when dry

habitat: Look for springs clearweed in consistently moist areas like spring seeps, wet meadow edges, and along small streams. It thrives in the soft, muddy soil where water stays near the surface year-round. You'll often find it growing alongside watercress, monkey flower, and other moisture-loving plants in partially shaded spots.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as tender, bright green shoots in moist soil. The translucent stems are most noticeable when plants are actively growing.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from July through September with tiny greenish flowers. This is the best time to identify the plant when it's at full size with visible flowers.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and the plant begins to decline. Look for the small, flattened teardrop-shaped seeds before the first frost kills the annual plant.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies completely back to the ground. Only seeds remain to sprout the following spring.

funFact: Springs clearweed belongs to the nettle family but has completely lost its stinging ability - it's like the family member who decided to become a pacifist while all its relatives stayed armed and dangerous!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close cousin Canada clearweed, which grows in similar wet areas. The key difference is in the seeds - springs clearweed has wider, more teardrop-shaped seeds while Canada clearweed's are narrower and more oval. Remember: springs clearweed has 'plumper' seeds like a teardrop.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the nettle family (Urticaceae), clearweeds are completely harmless to touch, unlike their stinging nettle relatives. The name 'lesser clearweed' used in some guides refers to it often being smaller than Canada clearweed, though the two can be very similar in size.
compareHints: Springs clearweed is nearly identical to Canada clearweed in appearance and habitat, making them one of the trickiest plant pairs to distinguish in New England. The most reliable way to tell them apart is by examining the mature seeds - springs clearweed produces wider, more teardrop-shaped seeds that are about 75-85% as wide as they are long. Both species have the same translucent stems and tiny flowers, so seed shape is your best bet for a positive identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada clearweed is much more common than its relative springs clearweed, which prefers wetter conditions near actual springs and streams.

Unlike its New England relatives Canada clearweed and springs clearweed, Artillery Plant has much smaller, more succulent-feeling leaves and stems, and lacks the translucent "windows" in the stems that give other clearweeds their name.
